routes.label: Complete the square and test smaller candidates

question:
Let \(R,\) \(S,\) and \(T\) be squares that have vertices at lattice points (i.e., points whose coordinates are both integers) in the coordinate plane, together with their interiors.

The bottom edge of each square is on the \(x\)-axis. The left edge of \(R\) and the right edge of \(S\) are on the \(y\)-axis, and \(R\) contains \(\dfrac{9}{4}\) as many lattice points as does \(S.\) The top two vertices of \(T\) are in \(R \cup S,\) and \(T\) contains \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) of the lattice points contained in \(R \cup S.\) See the figure (not drawn to scale).

[Figure 1](figures/2022_AMC_10A_Q25_question_fig1.svg)

The fraction of lattice points in \(S\) that are in \(S \cap T\) is \(27\) times the fraction of lattice points in \(R\) that are in \(R \cap T.\) What is the minimum possible value of the edge length of \(R\) plus the edge length of \(S\) plus the edge length of \(T?\)
solution:
Count lattice points using one more than each side length. A square of integer side \(u-1\) has \(u\) rows and \(u\) columns, hence \(u^2\) lattice points including its boundary.

Write the side lengths of \(R,S,T\) as \(a-1,b-1,c-1\). The ratio \(a^2/b^2=9/4\) gives \(a=3k\), \(b=2k\) for a positive integer \(k\). The two squares share exactly the \(b=2k\) points on the shorter vertical edge. Therefore
\[
|R\cup S|=9k^2+4k^2-2k=k(13k-2).
\]
Since \(T\) contains one quarter as many points,
\[
4c^2=k(13k-2).\tag{1}
\]
In particular \(k\) is even: if it were odd, the right side would be odd and the left side even.

The fraction condition says
\[
\frac{|S\cap T|}{4k^2}
=27\frac{|R\cap T|}{9k^2},
\]
so \(|S\cap T|=12|R\cap T|\). Both overlaps contain lattice points: if either count were zero, the equality would make both zero, contrary to the top vertices lying in \(R\cup S\). If \(T\) lay wholly to the right of the axis, its overlap with \(S\) would be contained in its overlap with \(R\), contradicting the ratio \(12:1\). Thus its left edge is negative and its right edge is nonnegative. Put its left edge at \(x=-j\), so its right edge is at \(x=c-1-j\). Its top vertices lie in the two larger squares, so all its \(c\) rows fit in each overlap. The overlaps have \(j+1\) and \(c-j\) columns, respectively, counting the axis in both. Hence
\[
\frac{j+1}{c-j}=12,
\qquad 13j+1=12c.
\]
This forces \(c\equiv-1\pmod{13}\), meaning that \(c\) is one less than a multiple of \(13\). In remainder calculations, multiples of \(13\) may be discarded. Thus \(c^2\) has remainder \(1\), and reducing (1) gives \(4\equiv-2k\pmod{13}\). Equivalently, \(13\) divides \(2(k+2)\). Since \(13\) does not divide \(2\), it divides \(k+2\). Therefore \(k\equiv11\pmod{13}\): \(k\) leaves remainder \(11\) when divided by \(13\).

The positive even possibilities for \(k\) start \(24,50,76,\ldots\). At \(k=24\), (1) gives \(c^2=1860\), which lies strictly between \(43^2=1849\) and \(44^2=1936\). It cannot be a square. At \(k=50\), (1) gives \(c=90\), and \(13j+1=12c\) gives \(j=83\).

This candidate is feasible: \(R\) has side \(149\) on the right of the axis, \(S\) has side \(99\) on the left, and \(T\) runs from \(x=-83\) to \(6\) with height \(89\). Its top vertices lie in \(R\cup S\); its overlaps have \(84\cdot90=7560\) and \(7\cdot90=630\) points, in the required ratio \(12:1\).

Finally, \(c=\tfrac12\sqrt{k(13k-2)}\) increases with positive \(k\), so \((3k-1)+(2k-1)+(c-1)=5k+c-3\) increases as well. Excluding every smaller possible \(k\) therefore proves that the minimum sum is
\[
149+99+89=\boxed{337},
\]
choice B. Boundary lattice points are the reason for the extra row, column, and shared-axis correction.
